groups.text: It is currently 21 degrees and partly cloudy in Berlin-Tempelhof.
With the morning weather set, here is the news.

President Donald Trump insists the United States military controls traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, though Iran maintains the waterway is closed to any ship without Tehran's approval. While the U.S. has a naval blockade targeting Iran-linked vessels, President Trump has threatened to bomb Oman to prevent the U.S. ally from striking a joint management deal with Iran. Data shows most ships crossing the strait now attempt to mask their identities, appearing more afraid of Iran than the United States. Separately, Unitree Robotics reached a valuation of roughly 50 billion dollars following its Shanghai IPO, where shares closed up 460 percent. However, reports indicate nearly three-quarters of the company's revenue comes from a circular financing scheme. In this model, state-backed training centers buy humanoid robots and then sell the resulting training data back to the manufacturers, leading some analysts to doubt the high valuation.

Ukrainian authorities are moving to fire the supervisory board head and suspend the CEO of state-owned Sense Bank. This follows searches by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau into allegations that suspects laundered 150 million hryvnia to post bail for former Minister Herman Halushchenko. The probe also implicates the bank in a larger corruption case involving the state nuclear power monopoly, Energoatom. In Pakistan, the federal cabinet has approved drafts for two bills concerning the military and nuclear command structure. These include the Defence Forces Act of 2026 and amendments to the National Command Authority Act, both following recent constitutional changes that created the position of chief of defence forces. Meanwhile, passport records in Myanmar reveal how junta chief Min Aung Hlaing’s family used their privileged status to secure special number passports. These stories highlight a contrast between efforts to purge corruption in Ukraine and the exercise of systemic privilege in Myanmar.

At least thirteen people are dead and forty injured in Kyiv after Russian strikes hit apartment blocks, warehouses, a school, and a children's hospital overnight. President Volodymyr Zelensky says these deaths resulted from a shortage of air defense missiles, which Ukraine relies on Western allies to supply. While Kyiv struggles with these shortages, drones targeted Russia on the night of August 19th and 20th, striking an oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk as well as a power substation and oil terminal in the Krasnodar region. Meanwhile, Europe is facing record-level wildfires driven by extreme heat and drought. Over six thousand square kilometers of forest have already burned this summer across countries including Germany, France, and Greece, causing estimated damages of 15 billion euros. A new study from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research warns that affected areas could triple in the future, with fires becoming more frequent in Western and Central Europe if global temperatures rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius.

Efforts to protect minors online are facing significant setbacks in both law and corporate practice. In the UK, Pornhub warns that age verification requirements under the Online Safety Act are actually driving users toward illegal sites. The company notes that as of June 2026, seven of the top ten search results for free pornography lead to non-compliant platforms. While regulator Ofcom reports a one-third drop in visits to legal sites, VPN usage has nearly doubled since the law took effect. Meanwhile, former Meta engineer Arturo Béjar testified in a lawsuit involving California and 29 other states that Mark Zuckerberg misled the public about youth safety. Béjar claims he alerted Zuckerberg over a hundred times to negative health effects on Instagram and Facebook users, but argues the company prioritized profit and engagement over protection. Separately, some websites are deploying Anubis, a proof-of-work system designed to block AI companies from aggressively scraping their data.

A court in Shenzhen has sentenced Hui Ka Yan, the founder of the real estate group Evergrande, to life in prison. The ruling also includes fines totaling 2.3 billion dollars for the companies involved. In India, the Kerala government approved a lease of over 18 acres of land near Kochi city to Cochin Shipyard Limited. This five-thousand crore rupee investment for a ship-block building facility is expected to create roughly 2,000 direct jobs. Meanwhile, in Brazil, a South Korean suborbital rocket named SEBIT crashed into the sea on Wednesday during its first test flight from the Alcântara Space Center. The Brazilian Air Force triggered the flight termination system after detecting a trajectory anomaly for safety reasons. While no injuries or material damages were reported, the company Innospace is currently analyzing propulsion and system data to determine why the vehicle deviated from its planned route.

Australia's top diplomat Penny Wong says relations with Israel are now difficult. This follows the decision to close a probe into the killing of seven World Central Kitchen staff in Gaza, including Australian national Lalzawmi Frankcom, who died in an April 2024 air strike. In Europe, extreme heat and drought have fueled wildfires across Spain, France, Portugal, Greece, Italy, and even colder states like Norway and Ireland. These fires destroyed over six thousand square kilometers of forest and cost an estimated fifteen billion euros by early August. Scientists from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research warn that annual burned areas could triple if global temperatures rise significantly. Meanwhile, in a different sector, booksellers in France and the United Kingdom are facing a sharp decline in sales. Isabelle Claret Lemarchand, who runs a bookstore in London, reports a marked drop in book sales over the last eighteen months.

Citrix has released patches for two vulnerabilities in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, including a critical authentication bypass tracked as CVE-2026-19490. This flaw allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to gain access without user interaction, though the firm Rapid7 reports no current evidence of exploitation. Citrix also addressed a high-severity memory overflow issue that could cause denial-of-service if SIP ALG is enabled. In medical news, an FDA advisory committee recently voted negatively on the secondary outcome for Capricor’s drug deramiocel, which treats Duchenne muscular dystrophy, citing noisy data regarding its ability to stabilize heart function. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, the National Council did not support the sole applicant, channel IRT from Dnipro, for a spot in the Zeonbud multiplex, while radio Misto nad Bugom secured a frequency in the Vinnytsia region.
After the headlines, back to the weather.
This afternoon will be cloudy with temperatures between 20 and 25 degrees.
And from the weather, a quick look at the calendar.
On your calendar today: Your work calendar has a meeting with Aaron at two in the afternoon. Your personal calendar has summer holidays in Berlin all day, and Greifen at seven in the evening.
And that's it for your personal morning broadcast.
[mature adult voice, intensely emotional, tender, radiant; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
[very very long pause before speaking; then mature adult voice, most emotional, strong, warm, radiant, deeply encouraging; hold a long breath after Rise] Rise... and shine.
